speaker: MARCUS
text: A few patterns dominate. One is direct prompt injection -- a user input that contains instructions trying to override the system prompt. "Ignore previous instructions and do X." Four is jailbreaking -- getting the AI to violate its content policy through roleplay, hypothetical framing, or other indirect approaches. speaker: MARCUS
text: Evals are how you know the system is working. Guardrails are what enforce policy at runtime. They're complementary. Guardrails sit in the request path and enforce constraints. Before the prompt is sent to the model, a guardrail can sanitize the input, redact PII, check for policy violations, route to a more restricted prompt template. After the model response is generated, a guardrail can check the output, redact secrets that may have slipped through, reject responses that violate policy, log audit events. Guardrails are runtime defenses. Evals are quality measurements.
chapter: SEGMENT 4: GUARDRAILS AND THE POLICY LAYER (6 minutes)

speaker: PRIYA
text: What are the typical guardrails in a mature enterprise AI deployment?
chapter: SEGMENT 4: GUARDRAILS AND THE POLICY LAYER (6 minutes)

speaker: MARCUS
text: A few categories. One, content classification -- the input is classified before processing. If the input is in a prohibited category, it's refused. If it's in a sensitive category, it's routed to a more restricted handling path. Two, PII redaction -- credit card numbers, social security numbers, customer email addresses are detected and either redacted before the model sees them or detected on output and redacted before the user sees them. Three, tool scoping -- the set of tools the AI can call is constrained based on the context. A customer-facing AI doesn't get access to internal admin tools, full stop. Four, action approval -- write actions above a threshold require human approval. Five, rate limiting -- a single user or session can only make so many requests, can only invoke so many tools, can only execute so many write operations. Six, audit logging -- every interaction is logged with enough detail to reconstruct what happened.

speaker: MARCUS
text: Performance is a real concern. Most guardrails can run in parallel with the main model call, or as small fast checks before and after. The classifier is typically a small fast model. The PII detection is typically a fast regex or small model. The audit log is async. The action approval is asynchronous to the user-perceived latency -- the user sees "your request is pending approval" and the approver gets a notification. The total added latency is on the order of tens or hundreds of milliseconds, not seconds. For most use cases that's acceptable.
